sense: of citizens, not military or of the church

terms.comment: Of citizens among themselves: bellum cīvīle, civil war (Cic.; Caesar’s Bellum cīvīle); jūs cīvīle, the civil law, the private law of Roman citizens (Lewis & Short); civil rights are jūra cīvīlia (Traupman 194) or jūs cīvīle (Traupman 178). Civil as against military: nōn mīlitāribus sōlum sed cīvīlibus quoque mūneribus (Liv. 9.3.5, Lewis & Short). It also means political (see political), and from Augustus on, of a great man, affable, behaving as one citizen among others (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Cic. Sull. 85: cui ūnī togātō supplicātiōnem dēcrēverit (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Wearing the toga, the citizen’s dress in peace, and so as a noun a civilian, against a soldier: Cicero is the only civilian for whom the senate decreed a thanksgiving (Lewis & Short). Traupman gives togātus and prīvātus for civilian.
Inward, internal; with bellum, a war within the state, and Morgan–Owens’s first word for civil war (after Milton). As a noun, intestīna are the guts.

phrases.latin: genus bellī quod sit vidēs. ita cīvīle est ut nōn ex cīvium dissēnsiōne sed ex ūnīus perditī cīvis audāciā nātum sit.
phrases.english: you see what kind of war it is: civil, but born not of a quarrel among citizens but of the reckless daring of one desperate citizen.
